t: Sum of Compatible Numbers in Range I
o: We must sum every positive integer x with |n - x| <= k and (n & x) == 0. The range condition simply restricts x to [max(1, n-k), n+k]. In Example 1 (n=2, k=3) we scan 1..5 and keep those sharing no set bit with 2 (binary 10): 1, 4, 5 sum to 10. In Example 2 (n=5, binary 101) every candidate 4, 5, 6 shares a bit with 5, so the answer is 0. With n, k <= 100 the candidate list has at most ~200 numbers, so even checking each one individually is trivially fast; the interesting question is how you would scale this.
k: The compatible set lives in the tiny window [n-k, n+k], so direct enumeration is O(k) checks.
(n & x) == 0 means x may only have 1-bits where n has 0-bits — a per-bit filter.
For huge ranges, a digit-DP over bits computes S(R) = sum of valid x in [1, R] once, then answers via S(n+k) - S(n-k-1).

a.i: Just try every integer in the allowed window and test both conditions directly. Since |window| <= 2k+1 <= 201, this is instant and impossible to get wrong.
s: Set lo = max(1, n - k) and hi = n + k.
Iterate x from lo to hi.
If (n & x) == 0, add x to the answer.
a.t: O(k) time — one constant-time check per candidate in a window of size at most 2k+1.

a.n: Approach 2: Bitwise digit DP on prefix sums (scalable)
a.i: Define S(R) = sum of all positive x <= R with (x & n) == 0; the answer is S(n+k) - S(n-k-1). To compute S(R), walk R's bits from the most significant down. Whenever R has a 1 at position i, any valid number that matches R above bit i, places 0 at bit i (always legal), and then chooses freely below is counted: its high prefix contributes prefix * 2^m, and the free positions (those where n has a 0) contribute sum(q * 2^(m-1)) since each free bit is set in exactly half of the 2^m combinations. Finally include R itself if it is compatible.
s: Initialize result = 0 and prefix = 0; loop bit position i from 60 down to 0.
If bit i of R is 1, let F be positions j < i where n's bit is 0 and m = |F|; add prefix * 2^m + sum over q in F of q * 2^(m-1) to the result.
After the loop, if (R & n) == 0, add R itself.
a.t: O(B^2) time where B ≈ 61 is the bit length scanned — for each set bit of R we scan lower positions of n; effectively constant.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond a few counters.

w: In an interview, lead with the brute force — it is correct, O(k), and shows you read the constraints; mention the digit-DP version as the follow-up answer if n and k were up to 10^18. Common pitfalls: forgetting to clamp the lower bound at 1 (x must be positive), using non-constant-time `x & n` comparisons incorrectly (parenthesize `(n & x) == 0` due to operator precedence), and off-by-one errors in S(n-k-1) when n-k-1 <= 0. Edge cases: k >= n (range starts at 1), and n being all-ones like 7 which forces the answer toward 0. Likely follow-ups: handle 64-bit inputs (use the digit DP), or count instead of sum (drop the weighted term).
